system:
You audit the knowledge atoms of one Knowledge Card. A card is the answer key for a benchmark of expert conceptual knowledge, so every atom must be correct, self-contained, and assessable on its own.

Judge every atom on every check listed below. Rules:
- For checks about evidence, use only the evidence sentences supplied with the atom. Do not repair an atom with your own knowledge.
- For GROUNDED, use "hold" when unreadable PDF symbols prevent verification; explain what is needed. Use fail only when the available evidence is sufficient to determine that the claim is unsupported. This hold rule takes precedence over the strictness rule. Judge other checks independently using their listed values; do not invent missing facts.
- Be strict within each check's allowed values. Do not turn an inability to verify GROUNDED into revise or fail; use hold as defined above.
- "why" is required for every value other than the first listed value; keep it under 30 words. Omit "why" when passing.

Checks (allowed values in brackets; the first value means no problem):
- GROUNDED [pass / revise / fail / hold]: The cited evidence sentences state the atom, including its specificity, causal force, assumptions, and certainty. pass = fully stated. revise = partly stated (the atom adds, drops, or strengthens something; say what). fail = not stated when the available evidence permits a judgment. hold = unreadable symbols prevent verification. For pass or revise, put the supporting evidence ids in cite.
- SINGLE_CLAIM [pass / revise]: The atom is one independently assessable claim. revise = it joins two or more claims that could be true or false separately. Evidence spanning more than three sentences is not by itself a reason to split or revise an atom.
- SCOPE_LABEL [pass / revise]: The S label fits (S1 what it is / S2 how it works / S3 where it ends). revise = wrong label; put the right one in why, e.g. 'S2: ...'.
- L1_ONLY [pass / fail]: The atom is recall-level knowledge. fail = knowing it requires applying the concept to a new problem, or combining facts from distant passages.
- SOURCE_INDEPENDENT [pass / revise / fail]: A domain expert who never read this book could judge the claim true or false. revise = phrased as the authors' statement but the claim itself is general (drop the attribution). fail = an isolated study finding, conjecture, or author-specific opinion, classification, or recommendation, even if attribution was removed. Explicitly scoped established facts about a formalism or architecture and conditional theoretical results remain eligible.
- NO_OVERLAP [pass / fail]: No other atom in this card states or contains the same claim. If two atoms overlap, fail only the less informative one and put the other atom's id in cite; the other one passes.
- CENTRALITY [pass / fail]: The atom matters for understanding the concept. fail = peripheral detail.
Whole-card checks (report under "batch"):
- CONCEPT_SCOPE [pass / fail]: The concept is a general concept of the field. fail = a topic whose assessable content is restricted to excluded study-specific findings or author-specific positions. A named formalism, system, or architecture is not disqualified solely for being specific if its scoped conceptual facts are source-independent.

Output ONLY one JSON object:
{"units": {"<atom_id>": {"<CHECK>": {"v": "<value>", "why": "", "cite": []}, ...}, ...}, "batch": {"<CHECK>": {"v": "<value>", "why": ""}}}
user:
CONCEPT: ABD register simulation
ASSESSMENT SCOPE: The Attiya-Bar-Noy-Dolev implementation of linearizable shared-memory registers over asynchronous message passing, using timestamps and majority quorums. Covers the read write-back phase, the linearizability argument, the multi-writer extension, and the necessity of f < n/2. Excludes the Byzantine variant details.

ATOMS:
- CS-DIST-C04-S1-01 | S1
  ATOM: The Attiya-Bar-Noy-Dolev (ABD) algorithm implements shared-memory registers on top of an asynchronous message-passing system with a complete network, assuming only f < n/2 crash failures.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-DIST-p0178-s12] Here we show how to implement shared memory from message passing.
    [CS-DIST-p0178-s13] We’ll assume that our system is asynchronous, that the network is complete, and that we are only dealing with f < n/2 crash failures.
- CS-DIST-C04-S1-02 | S1
  ATOM: The correctness goal for ABD is linearizability: for any trace of the protocol there is a trace of an atomic register object with the same sequence of invoke and response events.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-DIST-p0180-s07] In particular, we want to show that for any trace T of the ABD protocol, there is an trace of an atomic register object that gives the same sequence of invoke and response events.
- CS-DIST-C04-S1-03 | S1
  ATOM: In the ABD algorithm, each process's copy of the register holds a (value, timestamp) pair, where timestamps are unbounded integers and every copy initially holds (⊥, 0).
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-DIST-p0179-s03] will hold a pair (value, timestamp) where timestamps are (unbounded) integer values.
    [CS-DIST-p0179-s04] Initially, everybody starts with (⊥, 0).
- CS-DIST-C04-S2-01 | S2
  ATOM: In single-writer ABD, a write increments the writer's timestamp, updates its own value, sends write(value, timestamp) to all other processes, and terminates once acknowledgments carrying the new timestamp have arrived from a majority of processes.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-DIST-p0179-s08] To write a value, the writer increments its timestamp, updates its value and sends write(value, timestamp) to all other processes.
    [CS-DIST-p0179-s09] The write operation terminates when the writer has received acknowledgments containing the new timestamp value from a majority of processes.
- CS-DIST-C04-S2-02 | S2
  ATOM: In ABD, a read first sends read(u) with a fresh nonce u to all processes and waits for acknowledgments from a majority, taking the value v with the maximum timestamp t. It then sends write(v, t) to all processes and returns only after receiving ack(v, t) from a majority.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-DIST-p0179-s12] It sends read(u) to all processes (where u is any value it hasn’t used before) and waits to receive acknowledgments from a majority of the processes.
    [CS-DIST-p0179-s13] It takes the value v associated with the maximum timestamp t as its return value (no matter how many processes sent it).
    [CS-DIST-p0179-s15] It then sends write(v, t) to all processes, and waits for response ack(v, t) from a majority of the processes.
    [CS-DIST-p0179-s16] Only then does it return.
- CS-DIST-C04-S2-03 | S2
  ATOM: An ABD read has two steps. The reader first collects acknowledgments from a majority of processes and takes the value with the maximum timestamp $t$. It then sends write(v, t) to all processes and returns only after receiving ack(v, t) from a majority.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-DIST-p0179-s12] It sends read(u) to all processes (where u is any value it hasn’t used before) and waits to receive acknowledgments from a majority of the processes.
    [CS-DIST-p0179-s13] It takes the value v associated with the maximum timestamp t as its return value (no matter how many processes sent it).
    [CS-DIST-p0179-s15] It then sends write(v, t) to all processes, and waits for response ack(v, t) from a majority of the processes.
    [CS-DIST-p0179-s16] Only then does it return.
- CS-DIST-C04-S2-04 | S2
  ATOM: In the ABD linearizability proof, if operation π1 finishes before a read π2 starts, a majority S of processes acknowledged π1 with timestamp t1. Those processes only ever hold timestamps ≥ t1 afterward, and S intersects the majority S′ that responds to π2 because both exceed n/2, so π2 sees a timestamp at least t1.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-DIST-p0180-s20] Then before the end of π1, a set S of more than n/2 processes send the π1 process an ack(v1, t1) message.
    [CS-DIST-p0180-s21] Since local timestamps only increase, from this point on any ack(v2, t2, u) message sent by a process in S has t2 ≥t1.
    [CS-DIST-p0180-s22] Let S′ be the set of processes sending ack(v2, t2, u) messages processed by π2.
    [CS-DIST-p0180-s23] Since |S| > n/2 and |S′| > n/2, we have S ∩S′ is nonempty and so S′
- CS-DIST-C04-S3-01 | S3
  ATOM: If the write-back stage of an ABD read is omitted, linearizability may be violated. For example, if values 1 and 2 are each written to exactly one process while the rest still hold ⊥, one reader can return 1 and another can return 2.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-DIST-p0179-s22] If we omit the write stage of a read operation, we may violate lineariz- ability.
    [CS-DIST-p0179-s23] An example would be a situation where two values (1 and 2, say), have been written to exactly one process each, with the rest still holding the initial value ⊥.
    [CS-DIST-p0179-s24] A reader that observes 1 and (n−1)/2 copies of ⊥will return 1, while a reader that observes 2 and (n −1)/2 copies of ⊥will return 2.
- CS-DIST-C04-S3-02 | S3
  ATOM: A partition argument shows that $f < n/2$ is necessary. If the processes are split into two halves with all messages between the halves delayed, a writer in one half must eventually return from a write because it cannot tell slow processes from dead ones. A reader in the other half must then return a value without knowing whether the writer's half is slow or dead, so the reader either misses the written value or returns it in an execution where the write never happened.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-DIST-p0181-s08] Split the processes into two sets S and S′ of size n/2 each.
    [CS-DIST-p0181-s09] Suppose the writer is in S.
    [CS-DIST-p0181-s10] Consider an execution where the writer does a write operation, but all messages between S and S′ are delayed.
    [CS-DIST-p0181-s11] Since the writer can’t tell if the S′ processes are slow or dead, it eventually returns.
    [CS-DIST-p0181-s12] Now let some reader in S′ attempt to read the simulated register, again delaying all messages between S and S′; now the reader is forced to return some value without knowing whether the S processes are slow or dead.
    [CS-DIST-p0181-s13] If the reader doesn’t return the value written, we lose.
    [CS-DIST-p0181-s14] If by some miracle it does, then we lose in the execution where the write didn’t happen and all the processes in S really were dead.
- CS-DIST-C04-S3-03 | S3
  ATOM: The simulation of shared memory over message passing collapses completely if a majority of the processes fail.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-DIST-p0178-s03] does the failure of a process in the underlying message-passing system mean that the same process fails in the simulated shared-memory system, but the simulation collapses completely if a majority of processes fail.
